summary: A pipeline and dashboard for analysing 4,322 submissions to the EU Digital Fairness Act public consultation. The pipeline runs Mistral OCR, heuristic page cleaning and paragraph quality scoring, gpt-5-nano topic extraction against a seven-topic schema plus 'emergent' topics, and clustering of 1,458 raw emergent labels into 224. Each annotation must carry a verbatim quote. The only quantitative check is that 99.1% of quotes string-match their source paragraph. Topic extraction accuracy and the consolidation step are not evaluated. The paper is about policy-document analysis, not software development.

claims.claim: Every extraction is grounded in a verbatim quote (99.1% match rate).
claims.evidence: §4.2 and §5: exact and fuzzy string matching against source paragraphs. This shows the quotes exist in the source, not that they support the assigned topic.

claims.claim: The pipeline surfaced stakeholder concerns that a fixed-taxonomy approach would have missed.
claims.evidence: No fixed-taxonomy run and no expert assessment of the emergent topics. The examples are hand-picked from 224 clustered labels.

claims.claim: The pipeline is domain-generic; adapting it requires only a prompt update and a new dataset.
claims.evidence: Only one consultation is processed. §5 itself says the cluster threshold and chunk-score threshold need per-dataset calibration and that manual review is required.

patterns.note: Verified links run from each extracted claim to a source quote (deterministic string match), not from a requirement to code. Grounding correctness is not evaluated beyond quote presence.
Stakeholder-input mining before drafting regulation is analogous to pre-spec discovery. There is no software context and no evaluation of whether analysts reached better or faster conclusions.

methodology.sample: 4,322 submissions to one consultation (259 PDFs, 4,066 web-form texts).
methodology.baselines: None. Prior clustering work is discussed but not run.
methodology.models: gpt-5-nano at temperature 1.0 via LiteLLM; Mistral OCR.
methodology.variance: None; a single extraction run at temperature 1.0.
methodology.languages: Natural-language submissions (languages not quantified). Not about code.

standards.peer_review: None stated (CC BY copyright block; venue not named).
standards.artifacts: Code and processed data on GitHub (thalesbertaglia/dfa-dashboard); live demo.

biases.detail: Quote-match rate is reported as validation of grounding, but it measures copy fidelity, not whether the topic label is correct or the quote supports it.
Emergent topics (Age Verification, Payment Processor Censorship, Digital Ownership) are highlighted without any evaluation of the 224 consolidated topics.
One extraction model at one temperature.
Policy consultation analysis; not software development with LLMs or agents.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None evaluated comparatively. OpenAI and Mistral APIs are used.

verdict_reason: Off-topic for a software-development harness KB. It is also a system description without an evaluation of extraction quality: the only number is a string-match rate, and the generality and 'fixed taxonomy would miss' claims are untested.
applicability: Does not transfer as evidence. By analogy only: if the team's pre-spec harness has an agent extract requirements or domain rules from stakeholder documents (content-provider specs, accreditation or clinical guidance), requiring a verbatim source quote per item and checking it deterministically is cheap and catches fabricated quotes. This paper also shows that such a check does not verify the interpretation; a human or test still has to.
